# Sharp triangle three-tail inequality and subset payment

Let \(K\) be any nondegenerate triangle, with centroid \(g\) and area \(V\).
For a nonzero continuous linear functional \(u\), write
\[
 F(s)=V^{-1}|K\cap\{u(x-g)\ge s\}|.
\]
Then, for every real \(s\),
\[
 F(0)+F(s)+\frac79F(-s)\ \ge\ \frac{11}{9}.             \tag{1}
\]
The coefficient \(7/9\) is sharp in the formulation
\(F(0)+F(s)\ge4/9+c[1-F(-s)]\).
This strengthens the previously proved \(c=1/2\) inequality specifically
for triangles; no higher-dimensional strengthening is asserted.

An actual-source consequence is equally sharp: if \(E\subset K\) is
measurable with area \(e\), the sources \(E,K,K\), at integer bases
\(-1,0,1\), have at the actual middle centroid an all-halfspace lower bound
\[
 \operatorname{depth}_{E,K,K}(0,g)
       \ \ge\ \frac49V+\frac79e.                     \tag{2}
\]
This is absolute, unnormalized depth. The same statement holds with the
integer bases reversed. The set \(E\) need not have centroid \(g\).

## 1. Normalize every triangle direction

Apply an affine change from the standard triangle
\(T=\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,e_2)\) to \(K\), and permute its vertices so
that their functional values are increasing. Subtract the least value
and divide by the sum of the two remaining values. The three vertex
values are then
\[
 0,\ x,\ 1-x,\qquad 0\le x\le\tfrac12.
\]
Their centroid value is \(1/3\); every original real shift is transformed
to a real shift. Thus it suffices to consider this one-parameter family.
Put \(v=1-x\), and let \(f_x(q)\) denote the cap fraction above threshold
\(q\). For \(0<x<1/2\),
\[
 f_x(q)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&q\le0,\\
 1-q^2/[x(1-x)],&0\le q\le x,\\
 (1-x-q)^2/[(1-x)(1-2x)],&x\le q\le1-x,\\
 0,&q\ge1-x.
 \end{cases}                                         \tag{3}
\]
These are the areas of the removed origin triangle and retained last
vertex triangle. The formulas and their first threshold derivatives
agree at the internal interface. The cases \(x=0,1/2\) are their
continuous limits. Closed cut lines have zero area throughout.

With \(q=1/3+s\), (1) is precisely
\[
 W_x(q):=9f_x(q)+7f_x(2/3-q)+9f_x(1/3)-11\ge0.        \tag{4}
\]
The rest of this proof is a finite exact quadratic check over all
real thresholds and directions.

## 2. Directions \(0<x\le1/3\)

Multiply (4) by the positive number
\[
 D=x(1-x)(1-2x),
\]
and write \(N_x(q)=D W_x(q)\). The threshold breakpoints, in order, are
\[
 x-\tfrac13,\quad0,\quad x,\quad\tfrac23-x,\quad
 \tfrac23,\quad1-x.                                  \tag{5}
\]
The values of \(N_x\) at these six points are respectively
\[
\begin{split}
 &x(5x^2-6x+2),\\
 &x(108x^2-96x+25)/9,\\
 &x(207x^2-135x+25)/9,\\
 &x(15x^2-7x+1),\\
 &x(10x^2-6x+1),\\
 &x^3.
\end{split}                                         \tag{6}
\]
They are positive: the first polynomial decreases to a positive value
on this interval, and the four remaining nonconstant quadratics have
positive leading coefficient and negative discriminant.

On the five successive bounded intervals in (5), the coefficients of
\(q^2\) in \(N_x\) are
\[
 7x,\quad25x-9,\quad16x,\quad23x-7,\quad9x.            \tag{7}
\]
The first quadratic has its minimum at the left endpoint; the last has
its minimum at the right endpoint. The second is concave. The fourth
is concave when \(23x-7\le0\); when it is convex, its stationary point
is at or beyond its right endpoint, since
\[
 \tfrac23-q_*=\frac{3x(3x-1)}{23x-7}\le0.
\]
Thus these four intervals are covered by (6).

On the central interval both caps use the last proper branch of (3).
If \(N_x(q)=Aq^2+Bq+C\), direct expansion gives
\[
 A=16x>0,\qquad4AC-B^2=176x^4\ge0.                  \tag{8}
\]
This proves nonnegativity on the entire real line for that quadratic,
in particular on its required interval.

Outside (5), one cap is full and the other empty. The two constant
values of \(W_x\) are \(9f_x(1/3)-2\) and \(9f_x(1/3)-4\).
Both are nonnegative: explicitly
\[
 f_x(1/3)=\frac49+\frac{x^2}{9(1-x)(1-2x)}\ge\frac49.
\]
This treats all real \(q\) in the first direction range.

## 3. Directions \(1/3\le x<1/2\)

The six breakpoints are now
\[
 0,\quad x-\tfrac13,\quad\tfrac23-x,\quad x,\quad
 1-x,\quad\tfrac23.                                  \tag{9}
\]
Their \(N_x\) values are \(2x-1\) times, respectively,
\[
\begin{split}
 &7x^2-7x+1,\\
 &16x^2-13x+2,\\
 &30x^2-26x+5,\\
 &(270x^2-210x+37)/9,\\
 &(108x^2-87x+16)/9,\\
 &5x^2-5x+1.
\end{split}                                         \tag{10}
\]
Each displayed quadratic is convex and negative at both \(1/3\) and
\(1/2\). It is therefore negative throughout; multiplying by
\(2x-1<0\) proves endpoint nonnegativity.

The quadratic coefficients on the five bounded intervals are
\[
 9(2x-1),\quad25x-9,\quad16(2x-1),\quad23x-7,\quad
 7(2x-1).                                           \tag{11}
\]
The first, third and fifth quadratics are concave. The second either
is concave or has its stationary point outside the interval, unless
\(x\ge3/8\). When that stationary point belongs to the interval, its
discriminant test is
\[
 4AC-B^2
   =4(2x-1)(238x^3-280x^2+95x-9)\ge0.               \tag{12}
\]
The fourth interval is convex with stationary point in the interval,
and its test is
\[
 4AC-B^2
   =4(2x-1)(178x^3-192x^2+65x-7)\ge0.               \tag{13}
\]
For completeness, the two cubic sign certificates are the following
exact Bernstein coefficient arrays. The first cubic, on \([3/8,1/2]\),
has coefficients
\[
 (-51/256,\ -155/192,\ -71/48,\ -7/4).
\]
The second, on \([1/3,1/2]\), has coefficients
\[
 (-2/27,\ -5/18,\ -11/18,\ -1/4).
\]
Under the affine rescaling of each interval to \([0,1]\), a cubic is
the sum of these coefficients times
\(\binom3k t^k(1-t)^{3-k}\). All four basis terms are nonnegative,
so both cubics are strictly negative. Since \(2x-1<0\), (12)--(13)
follow. This is an exact polynomial certificate, not a numerical
sampling argument.

The stationary-point qualifications used above follow directly from
\[
\begin{split}
q_*-(x-\tfrac13)
  &=-\frac{3(2x-1)(3x-1)}{25x-9},\\
(\tfrac23-x)-q_*
  &=-\frac{2(2x-1)(8x-3)}{25x-9}
\end{split}
\]
on the second interval. On the fourth interval,
\[
\begin{split}
q_*-x&=-\frac{2(2x-1)(24x-7)}{3(23x-7)},\\
(1-x)-q_*&=-\frac{7(2x-1)(3x-1)}{3(23x-7)}.
\end{split}
\]
Their signs give exactly the stated ranges.

Outside (9) the same two constant cap sums as in Section 2 apply.
Here \(f_x(1/3)=1-[9x(1-x)]^{-1}\ge1/2>4/9\).
This proves (4) for all real \(q\). Continuity supplies \(x=0,1/2\)
and the shared interfaces, completing (1).

## 4. Actual subset payment, vertical caps, and sharpness

Translate \(g\) to zero. A nonvertical cap through the middle centroid
cuts the large endpoint at threshold \(s\) and the small endpoint at
threshold \(-s\), for one common nonzero functional \(u\). Set
\[
 B=V[1-F(-s)].
\]
The small endpoint contributes at least \((e-B)_+\). Equation (1)
gives \(V[F(0)+F(s)]\ge4V/9+7B/9\). Consequently its actual total
cap mass is at least
\[
 \frac49V+\frac79B+(e-B)_+
   \ \ge\ \frac49V+\frac79e.                         \tag{14}
\]
This keeps the same direction and the same opposing thresholds.
No independent per-fiber minimizing directions have been combined.

A closed vertical cap through the middle base contains the whole
middle fiber and at least one endpoint. Its retained mass is at least
\(V+e\), which exceeds (2). A containing cap can be translated parallel
to itself until it passes through the selected point, so (2) holds
for all containing halfspaces. Null continuous cut boundaries remain
null for \(E\), because its measure is dominated by area on \(K\).

Both constants are sharp. On \(T\), use \(u(x-g)=x_1-1/3\) and
\(s=1/12\). Then
\[
 F(0)=4/9,\qquad F(s)=49/144,\qquad F(-s)=9/16,
\]
and (1) is equality. To make (2) equality, take the actual convex
subset \(E=T\cap\{x_1\le1/4\}\), whose area is \(7V/16\).
The ambient cap
\[
 x_1-\frac{z}{12}\ge\frac13
\]
has zero area in \(E\) at base \(-1\), fraction \(4/9\) in the middle
triangle, and fraction \(49/144\) at base \(1\). Its mass is exactly
\(113V/144=4V/9+(7/9)(7V/16)\).
The midpoint inclusion \((E+T)/2\subset T\) ensures these are the
exact three fibers of an actual convex hull. Thus sharpness is also
an actual compatible-source statement.
